items.paragraph: Reviews of film adaptations often turn on fidelity: whether the film kept the plot, the characters and the ending of the book. The criterion is natural but confused. items.paragraph: Slang tends to age quickly, and the reason lies in what it is for. A slang word marks its users as insiders: to say it is to show that one belongs to a particular group, often a young one, and knows its current code. items.paragraph: A popular answer to the question of what makes someone the same person over time is memory: I am the person who did the things I can remember doing. The view has real appeal, since it explains why amnesia seems to threaten the self in a way that losing a limb does not. But it struggles with ordinary forgetting. I remember nothing of being two years old, yet I do not think the toddler in the old photographs was someone else. Defenders reply that a chain of overlapping memories, each linking to the one before, is enough. That repair helps, but it quietly concedes the original point: it is not remembering that makes me the same person, but something continuous of which remembering is only one part.

options.A: Citing an abstract painter's hidden technical skill accepts the critic's premise that worth tracks difficulty, whereas such work is valued for deliberate choices that a chance likeness cannot equal.
options.B: Abstract paintings are harder to make than realistic ones, since deciding what to leave out of a canvas calls for greater skill than drawing a likeness.
options.C: Abstract art cannot really be told apart from the work of children, which shows that its value depends wholly on the reputation of the painter who signs it.
options.D: Abstract painters deserve respect because most of them could draw a perfect likeness, and their simple canvases conceal years of demanding technical training.

items.paragraph: 'A child could have painted that' is the oldest complaint against abstract art, and defenders usually reply that the painter could also draw a perfect likeness and chose not to. The reply concedes too much. It accepts the critic's assumption that a picture is valuable in proportion to the difficulty of making it, and merely insists that the difficulty lies elsewhere, in the years of training behind the apparent simplicity. But much of what matters in such work is not difficulty at all; it is the decision about what to leave out, the sense of when a canvas is finished, the placing of a single shape so that it holds a whole surface. A child might produce something similar by accident, as a monkey at a keyboard might type a line of verse, without the result being the same kind of achievement. The complaint is answered not by proving the painter skilful but by showing that skill was never the right measure.
